stem: Mira explains to Jonas what “Linux” means in the strict sense. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Linux is a complete operating system that the GNU project wrote as one single program from scratch.
options.rationale: The GNU project wrote many userspace tools, but Linux itself is only the kernel.

options.text: Linux is a desktop environment that runs on top of the Ubuntu kernel.
options.rationale: Desktops such as GNOME are userspace programs; they run on the Linux kernel, not the other way round.

options.text: Linux is the kernel; the shell, the tools and the desktop around it are userspace software.
options.rationale: The kernel is the part that talks to the hardware, and a distribution adds everything else.

options.text: Linux is a package format that both Debian and Red Hat use to install and update software.
options.rationale: Package formats are `.deb` and `.rpm`; they are not Linux itself.

explanation: Linux is the kernel: it manages hardware, memory and processes. Userspace (shell, tools, libraries, desktop) and a package manager come from other projects and are bundled by a distribution.

stem: Which job is done by the kernel and not by an ordinary userspace program?

options.text: Reading a script line by line and running its commands.
options.rationale: That is the shell’s job, and the shell is a userspace program.

options.text: Choosing the next process for the CPU and handing out memory.
options.rationale: Scheduling and memory management are core kernel tasks.

options.text: Listing the files of a folder when Jonas types `ls`.
options.rationale: `ls` is a userspace tool; it asks the kernel for the directory contents.

options.text: Drawing the windows and the panel of the desktop.
options.rationale: The desktop environment is userspace software.

explanation: The kernel schedules processes, manages memory, drives hardware and handles filesystems and networking. Everything you start yourself runs in userspace on top of it.

stem: Which parts of a Linux system belong to userspace? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The driver for the disk controller
options.rationale: Drivers are part of the kernel or its modules.

options.text: The `bash` shell
options.rationale: Bash is an ordinary program that you start and that asks the kernel for services.

options.text: The `ls` command
options.rationale: `ls` is a userspace tool from the GNU core utilities.

options.text: The memory manager
options.rationale: Managing RAM for all processes is a kernel task.

options.text: The process scheduler
options.rationale: Scheduling which process runs next is done inside the kernel.

explanation: Userspace is everything you start and use: shells, commands, libraries and applications. The scheduler, the memory manager and drivers are inside the kernel.

stem: The terminal asks the system for the name of its kernel. What does this command print?

options.text: GNU/Linux
options.rationale: `GNU/Linux` is what `uname -o` prints, the operating system name.

options.text: Debian
options.rationale: `uname -s` prints the kernel name, not the distribution.
`i686` is the machine type that `uname -m` prints.

options.text: Linux
options.rationale: `uname -s` prints the kernel name, which is Linux.

explanation: `uname -s` (`--kernel-name`) prints the kernel’s name. The distribution’s name is stored in other places, such as `/etc/os-release`.

stem: Which command, with one short option, prints just the name of the running kernel? Type the whole command.
explanation: `uname` prints system information. Its `-s` option (`--kernel-name`) prints the kernel name, here `Linux`; `-o` prints the operating system name.

stem: A userspace program such as `cp` needs to read a file from the disk. How does it get the data?

options.text: It asks the kernel through a system call, and the kernel talks to the disk.
options.rationale: Userspace programs never touch the hardware directly; the kernel does it for them.

options.text: It talks to the disk controller directly, which is faster than going through the kernel.
options.rationale: Userspace programs have no direct hardware access; only the kernel does.

options.text: It asks the package manager to fetch the file from a repository.
options.rationale: Package managers install software; they don’t serve file reads.

options.text: It loads its own private disk driver into userspace and uses that.
options.rationale: Drivers live in the kernel, so a program can’t bring its own.

explanation: System calls are the doorway between userspace and the kernel. Because every program goes through it, the kernel can share the hardware safely.

stem: Ada wants a Raspberry Pi board for the studio’s test lab. Which statement about its official operating system, Raspberry Pi OS, is correct?

options.text: It is Enterprise Linux-based, so it uses `.rpm` packages and `dnf`.
options.rationale: The RPM-based families are Enterprise Linux and SUSE; Raspberry Pi OS isn’t one of them.

options.text: It is Alpine-based, so it uses `.apk` packages.
options.rationale: Alpine is a separate family with its own tools, and Raspberry Pi OS doesn’t use it.

options.text: It is Debian-based, so it uses `.deb` packages and `apt`.
options.rationale: Raspberry Pi OS belongs to the Debian family.

options.text: It is SUSE-based, so it uses `zypper`.
options.rationale: `zypper` belongs to SUSE-based distributions.

explanation: Debian GNU/Linux, Ubuntu and Raspberry Pi OS are the Debian-based distributions to know. They share the `.deb` format and the `dpkg` and `apt` tools.

stem: TuxPixel’s accountant asks which distribution is a free, community-driven system that aims to be compatible with Red Hat Enterprise Linux. Which one fits?

options.text: Alpine Linux
options.rationale: Alpine is its own family, built around musl and BusyBox, and isn’t a RHEL rebuild.

options.text: Rocky Linux
options.rationale: Rocky Linux (like AlmaLinux) is a free RHEL-compatible distribution.

options.text: openSUSE Tumbleweed
options.rationale: Tumbleweed is SUSE’s rolling release and has no RHEL compatibility goal.

options.text: Raspberry Pi OS
options.rationale: It is a Debian derivative for Raspberry Pi boards.

explanation: AlmaLinux and Rocky Linux are free alternatives for people who want RHEL compatibility without paying Red Hat for support.

stem: Which statement describes the relationship between Fedora Linux and Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL)?

options.text: Fedora is the community distribution that gets new things first; RHEL is developed from it.
options.rationale: Fedora sits upstream of RHEL in the Enterprise Linux family.

options.text: Fedora is a free rebuild of RHEL that appears some weeks after each RHEL release.
options.rationale: Rebuilds are AlmaLinux and Rocky Linux; Fedora is upstream, not a copy.

options.text: Fedora is the paid support edition of RHEL that companies buy for their production servers, with a contract.
options.rationale: Support subscriptions are sold by Red Hat for RHEL; Fedora is a community project.

options.text: Fedora is a Debian derivative that only borrows RHEL’s installer and logo.
options.rationale: Fedora belongs to the Enterprise Linux family and uses `.rpm` packages.

explanation: Fedora Linux tries new software first, CentOS Stream tracks the upcoming RHEL minor releases, and RHEL is the commercial product that follows.

stem: Which statement about openSUSE Leap and openSUSE Tumbleweed is correct?

options.text: Both are rolling releases, and only SUSE Linux Enterprise has numbered versions, as a commercial product.
options.rationale: Only Tumbleweed is rolling; Leap has numbered releases.

options.text: Tumbleweed is the fixed release and Leap is the rolling one.
options.rationale: It is the other way round: Leap is fixed, Tumbleweed rolls.

options.text: Both are Debian-based and use `apt`.
options.rationale: The SUSE family uses `.rpm` packages and `zypper`.

options.text: Leap has numbered releases and shares its core with SLE; Tumbleweed is the rolling release.
options.rationale: Leap follows numbered releases, while Tumbleweed continuously delivers new snapshots.

explanation: The SUSE family has the commercial SUSE Linux Enterprise (SLE) and two free openSUSE releases: Leap (fixed versions) and Tumbleweed (rolling, tested snapshots).

stem: Mira wants the smallest possible base image for a container that runs a tiny game server. Which distribution is known for being tiny and uses `apk` as its package manager?

options.text: Rocky Linux
options.rationale: It is Enterprise Linux-based and uses `dnf`; its images are far bigger.

options.text: Alpine Linux
options.rationale: Alpine uses musl and BusyBox and is popular for small container images.

options.text: openSUSE Leap
options.rationale: It is SUSE-based and uses `zypper`.

options.text: Ubuntu
options.rationale: It is Debian-based and uses `apt`.

explanation: Alpine Linux is a small, security-minded distribution with its own package manager `apk`, which makes it a favourite base for containers.

stem: Mira checks which distribution the practice guest runs. What does this command print?
explanation: `/etc/os-release` describes the distribution. Its `ID=` line gives a short lowercase name, here `debian`, which is how Debian-based systems identify themselves.

stem: Jonas has used Linux Mint on his old laptop. Which family does it belong to?

options.text: The Enterprise Linux family, as a free rebuild of Red Hat’s commercial system.
options.rationale: Rebuilds of RHEL are AlmaLinux and Rocky Linux, not Mint.

options.text: The SUSE family, using `zypper`.
options.rationale: Mint uses apt like the rest of the Debian family.

options.text: The Debian family; it is built on Ubuntu, which is built on Debian.
options.rationale: Mint is based on Ubuntu, which is based on Debian.

options.text: The Alpine family, built on musl and BusyBox.
options.rationale: Alpine is a separate small distribution; Mint is a full desktop system.

explanation: Linux Mint is a popular desktop distribution built on Ubuntu, so it uses the Debian family’s `.deb` packages and `apt`.

stem: What was Scientific Linux?

options.text: A RHEL-compatible distribution for research labs; it reached its end of life in 2024.
options.rationale: It was a RHEL-compatible distribution for science, and it is discontinued.

options.text: A Debian-based desktop distribution made for teaching programming to schoolchildren in classrooms.
options.rationale: It was RHEL-compatible, not Debian-based.

options.text: A rolling release from the SUSE family that ships recent scientific software.
options.rationale: It followed Red Hat Enterprise Linux, not SUSE.

options.text: A stripped-down distribution for routers and embedded boards in laboratories.
options.rationale: Its audience was laboratories and research institutes.

explanation: Scientific Linux served labs that wanted a free system compatible with RHEL. Its version 7 reached end of life on 30 June 2024.

stem: Ada reads that “CentOS Linux” has ended. What does the CentOS Project offer now under the CentOS name?

options.text: CentOS Rolling, a Debian-based fork of the old system.
options.rationale: No such Debian-based product exists; CentOS belongs to the Red Hat family.

options.text: A new commercial support product that replaces RHEL.
options.rationale: RHEL is still Red Hat’s commercial product.

options.text: Nothing; the project closed and removed its software.
options.rationale: CentOS Stream continues, and old releases stay available.

options.text: CentOS Stream, which sits between Fedora and RHEL.
options.rationale: CentOS Stream continues the name, while AlmaLinux and Rocky Linux took over the job of free RHEL-compatible distributions.

explanation: CentOS Linux 8 reached end of life on 31 December 2021 and version 7 on 30 June 2024. CentOS Stream, the upstream of RHEL’s minor releases, is what continues.

stem: Jonas finds an old tutorial that mentions “Raspbian”. What is Raspbian today?

options.text: A fork of Fedora for Raspberry Pi boards.
options.rationale: The system is Debian-based, not Fedora-based.

options.text: A cloud service that rents Raspberry Pi boards.
options.rationale: Raspbian was an operating system, not a service.

options.text: The former name of the Debian-based Raspberry Pi OS.
options.rationale: The Raspberry Pi Foundation renamed Raspbian to Raspberry Pi OS in 2020.

options.text: A Raspberry Pi model with a faster CPU.
options.rationale: The Raspberry Pi is the board; Raspbian ran on it.

explanation: Raspbian was the Debian-based system for Raspberry Pi boards. Since May 2020 it is called Raspberry Pi OS.

stem: What does “LTS” mean in “Ubuntu 24.04 LTS”?

options.text: Latest Technology Snapshot: a daily build that carries the newest packages of the release.
options.rationale: Snapshots are not LTS; LTS is about long support.

options.text: Limited Test Series: an early version meant only for testers.
options.rationale: LTS releases are meant for production, not for testing.

options.text: Linux Terminal Server: a special edition for thin clients.
options.rationale: The letters stand for Long-Term Support.

options.text: Long-Term Support: it gets security updates for much longer than other releases.
options.rationale: LTS releases come every two years and have five years of standard security maintenance.

explanation: Ubuntu publishes a new release every six months, and every two years one of them is a Long-Term Support release with five years of standard security maintenance.

stem: Mira reads that Debian keeps three lines at all times. Which description of Debian’s testing line is correct?

options.text: It holds packages being prepared for the next stable release.
options.rationale: Packages move from unstable into testing and the testing line becomes the next stable release.

options.text: It holds the current stable release, with security fixes only.
options.rationale: That is stable.

options.text: It holds packages that are broken on purpose, so that testers can find bugs.
options.rationale: Packages in testing are candidates for release, not deliberately broken.

options.text: It is a rolling release that never becomes a stable release.
options.rationale: Testing is where the next stable release takes shape.

explanation: Debian keeps stable, testing and unstable (nicknamed sid). Software enters unstable first, then moves to testing, and testing turns into the next stable release.

stem: Ada’s build server needs five years of security updates without a reinstall. Which kind of Ubuntu release should she choose?

options.text: The interim release from the spring
options.rationale: Interim releases are supported for only about nine months.

options.text: An LTS release
options.rationale: Long-Term Support releases get five years of standard security maintenance.

options.text: The daily development build
options.rationale: Development builds are for testers and change constantly.

options.text: A beta of the next release
options.rationale: A beta is a pre-release test version, not a supported one.

explanation: Ubuntu’s interim releases are supported for only nine months. For servers that should run for years, choose an LTS release.

stem: What is a rolling release?

options.text: No numbered releases to upgrade between: you keep updating and get the newest packages.
options.rationale: Tumbleweed and Alpine’s edge branch are rolling.

options.text: A release that is supported for a much longer time than the normal releases are.
options.rationale: That describes Long-Term Support (LTS).

options.text: A release that comes out every six months on a fixed date and has its own version number.
options.rationale: That is a regular fixed release cycle, as used by Ubuntu and Fedora.

options.text: A release that is only available to testers, before the public version is ready.
options.rationale: Alpha and beta versions are for testers; rolling releases are for everyday use.

explanation: In a rolling release the system keeps moving forward with each update. That gives the newest software but less predictability than a stable or LTS release.

stem: In Alpine Linux’s release scheme, what is *edge*?

options.text: The oldest stable branch, which has the longest support.
options.rationale: Stable branches are named like `v3.x`; edge is the development branch.

options.text: A repository that holds only proprietary firmware.
options.rationale: Edge is a branch, not a firmware repository.

options.text: The stable branch that is replaced by a newer one every six months, together with all its packages.
options.rationale: New stable branches appear about every six months, but edge is the rolling branch they are cut from.

options.text: The rolling branch that the next stable branches are cut from.
options.rationale: Edge has its own main and community repositories, plus a testing repository.

explanation: Alpine has numbered stable branches (a new one about every six months) and edge, the rolling branch for development. The `main` repository of a stable branch gets about two years of support.

stem: Which of these are rolling releases? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Debian stable
options.rationale: Debian stable is a fixed release that changes little.

options.text: Ubuntu LTS
options.rationale: Ubuntu LTS has fixed releases every two years.

options.text: openSUSE Tumbleweed
options.rationale: Tumbleweed continuously delivers new, automatically tested snapshots.

options.text: openSUSE Leap
options.rationale: Leap has numbered releases.

options.text: Alpine Linux edge
options.rationale: Edge is the rolling branch of Alpine.

explanation: Rolling releases have no version to upgrade to. Tumbleweed and Alpine’s edge branch are the two in the exam list; Leap, Debian stable and Ubuntu LTS are fixed releases.

stem: Which statement about Android and Linux is correct?

options.text: Android is a Debian-based distribution whose users install software with `apt`.
options.rationale: Android has its own userspace and no `apt` for users.

options.text: Android has no kernel of its own; its apps run directly on the hardware.
options.rationale: Every Android device runs a Linux-based kernel.

options.text: Android uses a Linux kernel, but not the usual GNU/Linux userspace.
options.rationale: Android’s kernels are built from upstream long-term-support kernels plus extra patches.

options.text: Android is the same as Ubuntu, only with a touch screen on top.
options.rationale: Ubuntu uses the GNU userspace, Android doesn’t.

explanation: Android is built on the Linux kernel, but apps run in Android’s own runtime and there is no ordinary Linux userspace with `apt` or a shell for the user.

stem: Jonas can run `sudo apt install gimp` on his Ubuntu laptop. Why won’t the same command work on his Android phone?

options.text: Android phones have no kernel at all, so no commands can run on them.
options.rationale: Android runs on a Linux kernel.

options.text: Android’s userspace has no `apt` and usually no shell; it has its own app system.
options.rationale: The kernel is Linux, but the software around it is different.

options.text: `apt` only works on desktops that have a mouse attached and a graphical login.
options.rationale: `apt` has nothing to do with the mouse; it needs a Debian-family userspace.

options.text: Android uses the Enterprise Linux family, so it needs `dnf`.
options.rationale: Android is not part of that family.

explanation: Android is a Linux-kernel system with a different userspace, so you wouldn’t call it a Linux distribution in the desktop sense.

stem: Which statements about Android are true? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Its kernel is based on the Linux kernel.
options.rationale: Android kernels come from upstream Linux kernels with additions.

options.text: It is the Red Hat family’s mobile edition.
options.rationale: Android is developed in the Android Open Source Project, not by Red Hat.

options.text: It runs only on x86 desktop processors.
options.rationale: Android phones mostly use ARM processors.

options.text: Its apps run in Android’s own runtime, not in a GNU userspace.
options.rationale: Android replaces the usual GNU userspace with its own.

options.text: It uses `.deb` packages managed with `dpkg`.
options.rationale: Android apps are installed as Android packages, not `.deb` files.

explanation: Android shares the kernel with Linux distributions and nothing much else of the usual software stack.

stem: Ada reads “most phones run Linux”. Which part of those phones is the Linux part?

options.text: The graphical app store.
options.rationale: The app store is Android software, not Linux.

options.text: The GNOME desktop.
options.rationale: Android doesn’t use GNOME.

options.text: The `apt` repositories.
options.rationale: Phones don’t use `apt` repositories.

options.text: The kernel, which manages the hardware and processes.
options.rationale: The kernel is the shared part; the rest differs from desktop distributions.

explanation: It is the kernel that Android and distributions such as Debian and Ubuntu share.

stem: Why is Android usually not called a Linux distribution like Ubuntu?

options.text: It uses the Linux kernel but not the GNU/Linux userspace and tools.
options.rationale: A distribution bundles kernel, userspace and package manager; Android’s userspace is different.

options.text: It is entirely closed source and owned by one company, with no public code.
options.rationale: Android’s base is the open source Android Open Source Project.

options.text: It runs only on servers, never on phones or tablets.
options.rationale: Android runs on phones and tablets.

options.text: It has no package format, so apps are plain unpackaged files.
options.rationale: Android apps are packages too; the point is that they aren’t the Linux userspace’s.

explanation: Android is a different operating system built on the Linux kernel.

stem: Which part of Android is described as built from upstream long-term-support kernels plus extra patches?

options.text: The app runtime
options.rationale: Apps run in Android’s own runtime, which is separate from the kernel.

options.text: The kernel
options.rationale: The Android project builds its kernels from upstream Linux LTS kernels and adds patches.

options.text: The package manager
options.rationale: Android has its own app installation system, not a kernel patch set.

options.text: The home screen
options.rationale: The home screen is an app of the user interface.

explanation: Android’s link to Linux is the kernel. Everything above it, including the runtime and the apps, is Android’s own software.

stem: Jonas’ smart thermostat has one fixed job and no keyboard or screen for a shell. What kind of computer is this?

options.text: A virtual machine hosted in the cloud.
options.rationale: A VM is a software computer, not a built-in device.

options.text: An HPC cluster.
options.rationale: HPC clusters are large collections of servers.

options.text: An embedded system: a small computer built into a device.
options.rationale: Embedded systems run one dedicated job inside a product.

options.text: A desktop workstation.
options.rationale: A workstation is a general-purpose computer with screen and keyboard.

explanation: Embedded devices such as routers, TVs, cameras and thermostats often run Linux without the user ever seeing it.

stem: Why is Linux popular in embedded devices?

options.text: It is the only operating system that can run without a kernel.
options.rationale: Linux has a kernel; the argument is cost and flexibility.

options.text: It is free, can be shrunk to fit small hardware and runs on many processor types.
options.rationale: Those three properties suit makers of routers, TVs and similar devices.

options.text: It requires a monthly licence that includes support.
options.rationale: Linux is free to use.

options.text: It runs only on one type of processor, which keeps devices simple.
options.rationale: Linux runs on many processor types.

explanation: Because the source is free, a manufacturer can trim Linux down and adapt it to its chip without paying per device.

stem: Which of these are typical embedded Linux devices? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: A rack server in a data center
options.rationale: Servers are general-purpose computers.

options.text: A developer laptop
options.rationale: Laptops are general-purpose computers.

options.text: A home router
options.rationale: Routers commonly run Linux.

options.text: A smart TV
options.rationale: Many TVs run Linux inside.

options.text: A rented cloud instance
options.rationale: Cloud instances are virtual servers.

explanation: An embedded system has one fixed job inside a product, such as a router or a television.

stem: Ada builds a prototype for a sensor box on a Raspberry Pi. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is a small board often used for embedded projects, and Raspberry Pi OS is its official system.
options.rationale: The board runs Linux, and Raspberry Pi OS is Debian-based.

options.text: It is a cloud service that rents out Linux servers for a monthly fee per board.
options.rationale: The Raspberry Pi is a physical board.

options.text: It cannot run Linux because it has an ARM processor instead of an Intel one.
options.rationale: Raspberry Pi OS and other Linux systems run on it.

options.text: It is a Linux distribution made by Red Hat.
options.rationale: The board is made by the Raspberry Pi company, and Red Hat is unrelated.

explanation: A Raspberry Pi is a low-cost board that runs Linux and is popular for embedded and learning projects.

stem: A maker of smart speakers has little memory to spare in its devices. Which property of Linux helps most here?

options.text: It needs a minimum of 16 GB of memory, which keeps the devices fast.
options.rationale: Linux can be built to run in a tiny fraction of that memory.

options.text: It only runs on one processor type, so no adjustment is needed for the device.
options.rationale: Linux supports many processor types.

options.text: It always starts a full graphical desktop, so users see a friendly screen.
options.rationale: Embedded Linux devices usually have no desktop.

options.text: The kernel and tools can be trimmed to just the parts the device needs.
options.rationale: Because Linux is free and open, a maker can cut it down to fit.

explanation: Linux can be shrunk, adapted to many chips and used without a per-device fee, which suits makers of routers, TVs and speakers.

stem: What is cloud computing?

options.text: Keeping all data on the user’s own USB sticks and external disks, with nothing on the network.
options.rationale: That is local storage, not cloud computing.

options.text: Running programs only on a supercomputer in the same room as the user.
options.rationale: The cloud is rented over the network.

options.text: Renting servers, storage and databases over the internet instead of owning them.
options.rationale: You pay for what you use.

options.text: A kind of weather simulation software that runs only on Linux.
options.rationale: It is a service model.

explanation: Instead of buying machines, a company starts virtual servers in minutes and pays for the time they run.

stem: Which operating system do most of the servers rented in the cloud run?

options.text: Android
options.rationale: Android is for phones and tablets.

options.text: Linux
options.rationale: Most cloud servers run a Linux distribution chosen as the image.

options.text: Only embedded systems, never servers
options.rationale: Linux powers servers as well as embedded devices.

options.text: Windows, because Linux cannot run in virtual machines
options.rationale: Linux runs very well in virtual machines.

explanation: In the cloud you pick a Linux distribution as the image, start the server and pay for the time it runs.

stem: Ada needs a test server for two hours before a release. Why is a cloud instance a good fit?

options.text: She has to buy a physical server and wait for its delivery.
options.rationale: That is the opposite of renting in the cloud.

options.text: It needs an annual contract that cannot be cancelled.
options.rationale: Cloud capacity is typically rented by time used.

options.text: Cloud servers cannot be removed once started.
options.rationale: They can be removed in minutes.

options.text: She can start it in minutes and pay only for the time it runs.
options.rationale: The cloud rents machines by use.

explanation: The cloud lets you add and remove capacity as needed, and Linux is the usual system on those machines.

stem: Which statements about running Linux in the cloud are true? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The server only runs one distribution, chosen by the cloud provider.
options.rationale: You choose the image.

options.text: You pay for the time the server runs.
options.rationale: Usage-based pricing is typical.

options.text: You must buy the hardware first.
options.rationale: The provider owns the hardware.

options.text: You can choose a Linux distribution as the image of a new server.
options.rationale: Providers offer Linux images for new instances.

options.text: Cloud servers cannot be accessed over the network.
options.rationale: They are managed over the network.

explanation: Cloud providers rent virtual servers over the internet and offer many Linux distributions as images.

stem: Which of these is a typical use of Linux in the cloud?

options.text: Running as the single operating system of a rented physical phone in the provider’s office.
options.rationale: Phones are not what cloud providers rent out; they rent servers and storage.

options.text: Controlling the engine of one particular car.
options.rationale: That is an embedded use, not a cloud use.

options.text: Hosting web servers and databases in virtual machines or containers at a provider.
options.rationale: Most rented cloud servers run Linux.

options.text: Working only on a computer without any network connection.
options.rationale: Cloud computing is delivered over the network.

explanation: Web and internet services, databases and containers all run in data centers, mostly on Linux.

stem: Jonas’ phone runs Android and has the Google Play Store on it. Which statement fits best?

options.text: The Play Store is part of the Linux kernel and ships with every kernel.
options.rationale: The Play Store is an app, not a kernel part.

options.text: Android is entirely proprietary, so it contains no open source code at all.
options.rationale: The Android base system is open source.

options.text: Android’s base system is open source, but the Play Store and Google’s services are proprietary parts added on top.
options.rationale: The base is open, and the proprietary Google layer is separate.

options.text: Everything on the phone is open source, because Android uses the Linux kernel.
options.rationale: A Linux kernel doesn’t make every program on top of it open source.

explanation: The Android Open Source Project is open source, but a phone as sold usually carries Google’s proprietary layer (Play Store, services, apps) on top, so it is not fully open source.

stem: Mira’s friend uses openSUSE Leap and mentions YaST. What is YaST?

options.text: The package format that Alpine Linux uses for its software.
options.rationale: Alpine’s format is `.apk`.

options.text: The name of openSUSE’s rolling release branch.
options.rationale: The rolling release is called Tumbleweed.

options.text: A Debian front end for `dpkg` that resolves dependencies.
options.rationale: On Debian that job is done by `apt`.

options.text: SUSE’s own tool for installing and configuring the system, such as disks, users and software.
options.rationale: YaST belongs to the SUSE family and covers setup tasks.

explanation: YaST is the installation and configuration tool of the SUSE family (openSUSE and SUSE Linux Enterprise).

stem: How is Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) sold?

options.text: As a rolling release that has no version numbers.
options.rationale: RHEL has numbered releases.

options.text: As a commercial product with a subscription that covers updates and support.
options.rationale: Support and updates come through a paid subscription.

options.text: It is community-run, with no company behind it.
options.rationale: Red Hat is a company, and it sells RHEL.

stem: Ada’s server runs a stable release that has been in maintenance for a year. Which updates should she expect?

options.text: No updates at all, because stable releases are never changed.
options.rationale: Stable still gets security fixes.

options.text: A switch to the unstable line once a year.
options.rationale: Releases don’t move to unstable by themselves.

options.text: Security and bug fixes, while the programs keep their versions.
options.rationale: Frozen versions with fixes only.

options.text: New major versions of the desktop and the compiler every month.
options.rationale: New major versions are what rolling releases bring.

explanation: In the maintenance phase of a stable release the package versions stay frozen, and only security and bug fixes arrive.
